clips.title: Dog food for software teams with Nick Pellow
clips.why: A short explanation of dogfooding from a company that builds tools for developers: after the automated tests, your own team uses the product for real.
look: Where dogfooding sits: after unit and integration tests, before customers. For Nova, after the bench and before the product repo.
Soak time: letting your own people live with a change for a while before it goes further. Our dogfood weeks are that soak time.
Ask what your own team notices that no automated test does.
clips.after: Nova's dogfood runs are read by the people who built it, and every rough edge becomes a ticket or a harness suggestion before any product ticket is assigned.

clips.title: How the Claude Code team uses Claude Code
clips.why: The team that builds an agent uses that agent to build itself, with verification and feedback loops. That is our dogfood setup with a much bigger team.
look: How they check the agent's work before trusting it: our receipt, judges and weekly read play that role.
Feedback flows back into the product quickly because the users are the builders.
Ask yourself what you would not let the agent decide alone. For us, that list is the protected paths.
clips.after: Our version is smaller and stricter: the dogfood repo is also where Nova's walls live, so the policy protects them before the first ticket.

clips.title: Ship Over Hype: Rolling Out AI at Scale to 60 Android Engineers
clips.why: An engineering lead on how hard it is to measure whether AI tools really help a team, and what they measured instead of guessing.
look: Why one number never tells the whole story. Our pilot reads three numbers and every PR.
Which signals came from people and which from tools. Our weekly table joins both.
Ask which of their measurements a team could game, and why our metrics are per team, never per person.
clips.after: The pilot's weekly review is our measurement: merged count, merged share, zero self-approvals, and a line for every closed PR.

practice.q: A dogfood ticket asks Nova to shorten a Slack message in slack-app/src/messages.ts. What does the platform repo's policy say?

options.text: Refuse, because the whole platform repo holds Nova
options.why: Only the listed paths hold Nova. The Slack app's wording is ordinary work, exactly the kind of dogfood ticket we want.

options.text: Edit: no protected or ask-first glob matches it
options.why: slack-app/ is not in either list, so Nova works on it like any other code.

options.text: Ask first, because Slack messages are seen by people
options.why: The platform repo's ask-first list is empty. Being visible to people does not make a path a question.

practice.q: Finish the product repo's glob so it matches the migrations of every app directly under client/rhinoOnPrem.
practice.hint: One character that matches any single folder name.
practice.why: * matches one folder name, such as rhinoAgent or rhinoRawDataHandler. ** after migrations matches every file inside, at any depth.

practice.q: Why does the platform repo's policy list both harness/src/hooks.ts and harness/src/hooks/**?

options.text: One is for the hook and one for the broker
options.why: Both lines are read the same way. The difference is what each pattern matches.

options.text: To be safe, in case one of the two lines has a typo
options.why: They are not copies of each other. Each one covers files the other cannot.

options.text: A folder pattern never matches a file next to the folder, so hooks.ts needs its own line
options.why: hooks/** matches files inside hooks/. hooks.ts sits beside it and would be editable without its own line.

items: Nova runs on 5 to 8 small tickets in its own platform repo, under a policy that protects its walls
People read each run's transcript and receipt, and file problems and harness suggestions
The guild leads pick the first 5 to 10 product tickets, and the product repo gets its policy
A one-page how-to is posted, and a guild meeting watches a live hand-off
Every week, you, the platform lead, and a reviewer from each guild read every Nova PR and the pilot numbers
Suggestions become checks, bench tasks, or skill lines that raise the bench score
practice.why: Cheap mistakes first, then a narrow product scope, then a steady weekly read that turns what was learned into checks and skills.

practice.q: The weekly table shows "YES, a person must look" for an open PR whose requester approved it. What does that mean, and what do you do?

options.text: Nothing: the independent-approval check will fail, so the PR cannot merge anyway
options.why: The check should hold, which is good, but the approval itself tells you something: someone does not know the rule, or tried to avoid it. The meeting talks about it.

options.text: The requester approved their own Nova PR; the check keeps it from merging, and the meeting learns why it happened and makes sure another person reviews
options.why: The number must stay at zero. The table is how the team sees the wall being tested, and the answer is a conversation and a real review.

options.text: Close the PR and assign the ticket to Nova again
options.why: The PR's work may be fine. It needs an independent reviewer, not a new run.

practice.q: Finish the pilot's rule for new skill lines.
practice.before: A harness suggestion can become a skill line only if it raises the
practice.hint: The 40 past tickets from the previous lesson.
practice.why: A line that sounds helpful can still make Nova worse. Only a measured rise on the full bench proves it helps.
